ineq-claim-credits.title: Getting the tax credits my family is already owed
ineq-claim-credits.line: Each spring I get back the money the tax system sets aside for working families like mine.

fixes.title: Check whether you qualify for the tax credit for working families
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS estimates that about one in five people who qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit never claim it, and the average credit was about $2,541 for tax year 2022. The IRS has a free online EITC Assistant that asks a few questions and tells you whether you qualify.
fixes.firstStep: Open the IRS EITC Assistant and answer its questions using last year's income.

fixes.title: Have a trained volunteer do your taxes for free
fixes.whatChanges: The IRS runs free tax preparation sites for people who generally earn about $70,244 or less, and volunteers there know which credits people tend to miss. Most sites are open from January to April, so book early.
fixes.firstStep: Look up the nearest free tax site with the IRS locator tool and write down its hours.

fixes.title: Yearly reminders to claim the credits you're owed
fixes.whatChanges: Keeps a private note of the credits that fit your household and reminds you in January, when the IRS's free tax preparation sites open for the season, with the nearest site and what to bring.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and put a reminder in your calendar for early January to book a free tax appointment.

ineq-claim-credits.writerNotes: Basics sweep: unclaimed credits are the most common, concrete money left on the table.

ineq-fair-pay.title: Knowing whether I'm paid fairly for my work
ineq-fair-pay.line: I know what people doing my job around here earn, and I can ask for a raise with real numbers.

fixes.title: Compare pay with a coworker you trust
fixes.whatChanges: The Labor Department lists openly talking with coworkers about your wages, benefits and conditions as a right federal law protects for most private-sector workers, with or without a union. Pay gaps tend to last when nobody compares notes. Supervisors usually aren't covered.
fixes.firstStep: Ask one coworker you trust whether they'd be willing to swap hourly pay numbers.

fixes.title: See what your job pays in your area
fixes.whatChanges: Takes your job title and ZIP code and shows what people in the same work earn nearby, using the government's yearly wage survey, then helps you write a short, calm raise request. Your own pay stays on your device.
fixes.speculativeRationale: The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes occupational wage data by metro area each year; the page was not opened in this run, so this fix is marked speculative.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and write down your current hourly pay, including regular overtime or tips.

ineq-fair-pay.writerNotes: Relational lens. Legal right framed as what the Labor Department lists, not as legal advice; one limit (supervisors).

ineq-local-spending.title: Spending that keeps more money in my town
ineq-local-spending.line: More of what my household spends ends up with local businesses and the people who work there.

fixes.title: Move one regular purchase to a locally owned business
fixes.whatChanges: In Preston, England, six big local institutions agreed to buy more from nearby suppliers, and their share of spending inside the city rose from 5% in 2012/13 to 19% in 2016/17. That was large institutions, not households, so moving one of your own purchases is a much smaller version of the same idea.
fixes.firstStep: Pick one thing you buy every week, like coffee or groceries, and find a locally owned place that sells it.

fixes.title: Choose businesses owned by the people who work there
fixes.whatChanges: About 6,400 American companies have an employee stock ownership plan covering 15.1 million people, and those plans paid out more than $166 billion to workers in 2023. When you have a choice of plumber, grocer or brewery, picking an employee-owned one means buying from a business its workers partly own, though how much each plan pays them varies a lot.
fixes.firstStep: Next time you hire a service or try a new store, ask whether it's employee-owned.

fixes.title: Map of employee-owned businesses near you
fixes.whatChanges: Shows employee-owned and locally owned businesses near you, starting from public lists of companies with employee stock ownership plans, so you know where your regular spending could go. About 6,400 American companies have one of these plans.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and ask one local business you use whether it's owned by its employees.

ineq-local-spending.writerNotes: Basics sweep: where you spend. Preston reused at the together level below.

ineq-credit-cheaply.title: Building credit without paying high interest
ineq-credit-cheaply.line: I can borrow when I need to at a fair price, because I have a credit history that lenders trust.

fixes.title: Join a lending circle that reports to the credit bureaus
fixes.whatChanges: Mission Asset Fund in San Francisco turns the old custom of friends pooling money and taking turns into small loans that get reported to the credit bureaus. A Boston Fed study of members from 2011 to 2013 found that people who started with no score or a poor one were almost twice as likely to raise it by 20 points as similar people outside the program.
fixes.firstStep: Pull your free credit report and write down your score, or note that you don't have one yet.

fixes.title: Start a savings circle with people you trust
fixes.whatChanges: Many families already pool money this way and call it a tanda, susu or chit fund: each person pays in monthly and one person takes the whole pot each turn. Writing down the order and the dates keeps everyone on the same page.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Rotating savings groups are a long-standing practice in many communities; no specific source was opened for this fix in this run.
fixes.firstStep: Ask two or three people you trust whether they'd put in a small, fixed amount each month.

fixes.title: Private matching for savings circles
fixes.whatChanges: Lets you say privately that you'd join a savings circle at a certain monthly amount, and introduces you to others nearby only once enough people want the same, then keeps a shared record of the order and dates.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Threshold matching is an It idea built on the savings circle custom described on this card; no specific source was opened for the feature.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and decide the monthly amount you could put in without strain.

ineq-see-the-gap.title: Seeing how wide the gap is where I live
ineq-see-the-gap.line: I know how unequal incomes are in my county, whether the gap is growing, and what I could ask for locally.

fixes.title: Look up how unequal incomes are in your county
fixes.whatChanges: Shows your county's Gini index, a yearly inequality score the Census Bureau publishes for larger counties, where 0 means every household earns the same, along with how it has changed and what local choices are on the table. In 2024 San Bernardino County, California, scored 0.435, below the state's 0.485 and the country's 0.483.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and search data.census.gov for "Gini index" with your county's name.

fixes.title: Check which benefits and credits your household can get
fixes.whatChanges: Offers a short questionnaire wherever you live to check which benefits and credits your household can get, with your answers kept on your device. In Colorado, a free tool of this kind called MyFriendBen helped more than 55,000 households apply for $33 million in benefits within two years.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and gather last month's pay stubs so the questions go quickly.

fixes.title: Write to your representatives about a specific bill
fixes.whatChanges: Finds who represents you at the city, state and federal level and helps you write a short note, in your own words, about a bill on wages, taxes or savings for kids. USA.gov already lists those officials and how to reach them.
fixes.firstStep: Look up your state legislators on USA.gov and save their email addresses.

ineq-see-the-gap.writerNotes: It-led card. All three fixes are proposed It features grounded in public data or existing tools.

ineq-baby-bonds.title: Every child starting adult life with some savings
ineq-baby-bonds.line: Kids born into families like mine turn 18 with real money for school, a home or a business.

fixes.title: Ask your state lawmakers to start a baby bond program
fixes.whatChanges: Connecticut sets aside $3,200 for each baby born on the state's Medicaid program, invests it, and lets the child apply for it at 18 to pay for college, job training, a home or a business in the state. Supporters see it as a way to narrow the wealth gap from birth; others would rather spend the money on cash help for families now.
fixes.firstStep: Search your state legislature's website for "baby bonds" to see whether a bill has been filed.

fixes.title: Open a small savings account in your child's name
fixes.whatChanges: A baby bond is the public version of something some families do on their own: putting a little away every month so a child starts adulthood with a cushion. Even $10 a month adds up over 18 years.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Basic household practice; no specific source opened. Arithmetic only: $10 x 12 x 18 = $2,160 before interest.
fixes.firstStep: Ask your bank or credit union what kind of savings account they offer for children.

fixes.title: Alerts when your state takes up a baby bond bill
fixes.whatChanges: Watches your state legislature for baby bond bills, like the one that set aside $3,200 for each baby born on Connecticut's Medicaid program, and tells you when one gets a hearing or a vote so you can weigh in at the right time.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and sign up for your state legislature's email updates if it offers them.

ineq-baby-bonds.writerNotes: Contested: presents supporters' and critics' directions.

ineq-cash-floor.title: Steady cash so one bad month doesn't sink my family
ineq-cash-floor.line: If my hours get cut or the car breaks down, there's a small, reliable amount of money that keeps my family afloat.

fixes.title: Ask your city council to fund a guaranteed income pilot
fixes.whatChanges: In 2019 Stockton, California, gave 125 residents $500 a month with no strings attached, and after a year full-time work among them rose from 28% to 40%, more than in a comparison group. Philanthropy paid for it, and it was a small, one-year test, so a pilot where you live would be the real test.
fixes.firstStep: Email your city council member to ask whether the city has looked at a guaranteed income pilot, and whether they'd support one.

fixes.title: Tell your senators whether you want the larger child tax credit back
fixes.whatChanges: Congress made the child tax credit larger for 2021, and after that ended, child poverty under the government's supplemental poverty measure more than doubled, from 5.2% in 2021 to 12.4% in 2022. Other pandemic aid ended that year too, and people disagree about the cost and about whether monthly payments change how much parents work.
fixes.firstStep: Send each of your two U.S. senators a short note through their website saying where you stand on the child tax credit, and why.

fixes.title: Guaranteed income pilots near you and what they found
fixes.whatChanges: Lists guaranteed income pilots in your city, county or state, with who got money, how much and what happened, like the 2019 pilot in Stockton that gave 125 residents $500 a month, so you can point your council to real results.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and search your city's name with "guaranteed income pilot" to see what turns up.

ineq-cash-floor.writerNotes: Contested: limits and disagreement stated once each.

ineq-wage-boards.title: Wages set with workers at the table
ineq-wage-boards.line: People who do my kind of job help decide what the whole industry pays, not just one employer at a time.

fixes.title: Ask your state lawmakers to set up a wage board for one industry
fixes.whatChanges: Since April 2024, fast food restaurants in California that belong to chains with 60 or more locations nationwide have had to pay at least $20 an hour, with a few exceptions such as some bakeries. A state council can raise that by up to 3.5% a year, and the deal came from unions and the industry agreeing to it rather than one side winning outright.
fixes.firstStep: Email your state legislator to ask whether they'd support a council that sets wages for an industry like fast food.

fixes.title: Ask candidates what they make of the evidence on higher fast food pay
fixes.whatChanges: After California raised fast food pay to $20 an hour, a UC Berkeley study found pay rose about 18% on average, prices rose once by about 3.7%, and jobs held steady. Critics point to other data showing about 2,200 lost jobs, so asking which evidence a candidate trusts tells you a lot about how they'd decide.
fixes.firstStep: Write one question about higher wages for a single industry and send it to a state legislative candidate's campaign.

fixes.title: Shared campaign for a wage board in your state
fixes.whatChanges: Gathers workers and neighbors behind one ask, a state board that sets pay for one industry, keeps track of who has signed on and which lawmakers have answered, and sends the letters together once enough people are in.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Campaign organizing is an It idea; it relies on simple sign-on lists and legislator contact data, not on a specific opened source.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and ask two coworkers or friends in the same line of work whether they'd sign on.

ineq-own-workplace.title: Owning a share of the company I work for
ineq-own-workplace.line: When the business I work for does well, I get part of the gain, not just my wages.

fixes.title: Ask your boss what happens to the business when they retire
fixes.whatChanges: Project Equity, a nonprofit in Oakland, estimates that baby boomers own 2.34 million American businesses employing 24.7 million people, and one estimate says about 80 percent of those businesses have no plan for what happens next. Selling to the employees is one way to keep the jobs, and the owner still gets paid for the business.
fixes.firstStep: Ask your boss, casually, whether they've thought about who takes over when they step back.

fixes.title: Share how one founder handed most of his company to staff
fixes.whatChanges: In 2019 Julian Richer put 60% of Richer Sounds, a UK entertainment retailer with 53 stores, into a trust for its employees, and each of 522 staff got £1,000 for every year they'd worked there, about £8,000 on average. Owners are often more open to this when they hear how another owner did it.
fixes.who: You and a business owner you know
fixes.firstStep: Send the story to one business owner you know who's thinking about stepping back.

fixes.title: Private check on whether coworkers want to buy the business
fixes.whatChanges: Lets each coworker say privately whether they'd want the staff to buy the business someday, and shows the result only once enough people have answered, so nobody has to go first in front of the boss.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Threshold matching among coworkers is an It idea; no specific source was opened for the feature.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and quietly ask one coworker whether they'd ever want a share of the business.

ineq-pay-gap-at-work.title: Top pay that isn't hundreds of times bottom pay
ineq-pay-gap-at-work.line: The gap between what the boss earns and what I earn is something we can see and talk about.

fixes.title: Propose a cap on top pay compared with bottom pay
fixes.whatChanges: Mondragon, a federation of worker cooperatives in Spain's Basque Country, caps the gap between its highest- and lowest-paid people at 6 to 1 across nearly 70,000 member-owners. Not every worker there is a member, and its appliance maker Fagor went bankrupt after 2008, so the model isn't without trouble.
fixes.firstStep: If your employer is a public company, find the CEO pay ratio in its latest proxy statement.

fixes.title: Suggest your workplace publish its pay ranges
fixes.whatChanges: New York passed a law in 2023 that requires employers to publish salary ranges for jobs, and several other states have pay transparency laws of their own. Your workplace can choose to share the range for every role with its own staff, even where no law requires it.
fixes.firstStep: Ask your manager or HR whether the pay range for your role is written down anywhere.

fixes.title: Anonymous pay sharing among coworkers
fixes.whatChanges: Collects pay from coworkers privately and shows the range for each role only once enough people in that role have shared, so everyone can see the gap without anyone's own number being exposed.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Threshold pay pooling is an It idea; no specific source was opened for the feature.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and write down your role and hourly pay so you have them ready.

ineq-pay-gap-at-work.writerNotes: Culture lens: norms about pay visibility.

ineq-tax-top.title: The richest households paying more toward schools and transit
ineq-tax-top.line: Public schools and buses near me are paid for partly by the people who've gained the most.

fixes.title: Ask your state legislator where they stand on taxing million-dollar incomes
fixes.whatChanges: Massachusetts adopted a 4% tax in 2022 on household income above about $1.1 million a year, and in the year ending June 30, 2026, it brought in more than $3.38 billion. That money is meant only for education and transportation, such as free school meals and free community college.
fixes.firstStep: Call or email your state legislator's office and ask where they stand on taxing top incomes, and why.

fixes.title: Ask candidates how they'd keep wealthy residents from leaving over a new tax
fixes.whatChanges: When Norway set its top wealth tax at 1.1% in 2022, at least 30 billionaires and millionaires moved abroad that year, more than in the previous 13 years combined. Supporters and critics disagree about how much that cost the country, and a wealth tax is different from a tax on income.
fixes.firstStep: Write down one question about wealthy residents moving away and bring it to the next candidate forum or town hall near you.

fixes.title: Record of how your state lawmakers voted on tax bills
fixes.whatChanges: Summarizes your state lawmakers' votes and public statements on taxes for top incomes into a lasting record, so when you ask where they stand you can check what they actually did.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Accountability records are an It idea built on public legislative vote records; no specific source was opened for the feature.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and look up your state legislator's voting record on your legislature's website.

ineq-tax-top.writerNotes: Contested: two directions with named examples; no claim that one is right.

ineq-land-trust.title: An affordable home that stays affordable for the next family
ineq-land-trust.line: I own my home at a price I can manage, and when I sell, another family gets the same chance.

fixes.title: Buy a home through a community land trust
fixes.whatChanges: The Champlain Housing Trust in Vermont keeps the land and sells only the house, so the price doesn't include the land, and a study found sellers still gained about $12,000 on resale while the home stayed affordable for the next buyer. You build less wealth than in a booming open market, which is the tradeoff.
fixes.who: You and a local land trust
fixes.firstStep: Search for a community land trust in your area and check its income limits.

fixes.title: Ask your city to put public land into a land trust
fixes.whatChanges: Cities that own vacant lots or old buildings can hand them to a land trust instead of selling them, so the homes built there stay affordable for good. City council members decide this, usually with little public attention.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Champlain Housing Trust began with city support in Burlington (background knowledge, not confirmed on the opened page).
fixes.firstStep: Find your city's list of vacant city-owned property, or ask your council member's office for it.

fixes.title: Community land trusts near you and who qualifies
fixes.whatChanges: Finds community land trusts that sell homes in your area, with their income limits and waiting lists, and tells you which ones your household might qualify for, with your income kept on your device.
fixes.speculativeRationale: A land trust directory is an It idea; no national directory was opened in this run.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and write down your household's yearly income before taxes.

ineq-anchor-buying.title: Hospitals, colleges and city hall buying from local businesses
ineq-anchor-buying.line: The biggest employers in my area spend their money with local firms and co-ops, so the jobs stay here.

fixes.title: Ask your city to track how much it buys from local firms
fixes.whatChanges: In Preston, England, the city and five other big local institutions changed how they buy, and the share of their spending that stayed in the city rose from 5% to 19% in four years. Some critics ask whether local preference makes suppliers less competitive, which is worth raising too.
fixes.firstStep: Find your city's purchasing or procurement page and see whether it reports local spending.

fixes.title: Organize neighbors around one local buying goal
fixes.whatChanges: Helps a neighborhood group pick one goal, like getting the hospital to buy food from local farms, then keeps track of who's been contacted and what they said. Groups tend to stall when nobody remembers who promised what.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Organizing support is an It idea; feasibility rests on simple shared lists, not on a specific opened source.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you'd use this, and ask two neighbors which big local employer they'd most want to buy local.
